summary: This informational RFC discusses long-term reporting of IP network performance metrics, over hours to months, for two audiences with different needs, and how those audiences affect the metric parameters chosen.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6703 explains how the intended reader changes the way network performance measurements should be designed and reported. It covers long-term loss, delay, capacity, and the details needed to interpret results.

questions: how to report ip network performance metrics
who are the audiences for performance metrics
how long should a packet loss waiting time be
should lost packets have infinite delay
how should long-term ip performance be reported
subtitle: How to report long-term IP performance results for network operators and application designers.

tldr.problem: The same IP performance measurements are used to characterize networks and to estimate application performance, but these audiences need different interpretations and reporting choices.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC compares those two points of view and discusses how they affect loss, delay, capacity, test-stream design, and sample size in long-term reports.
tldr.outcome: The document recommends reporting loss and delay together, leaving lost-packet delay undefined, and describing variability in capacity results. It is Informational guidance, not a protocol.

facts.label: Suggested delay statistics
facts.value: Mean and median of packets that arrive

today: RFC 6703 is an Informational RFC published in August 2012. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it provides reporting considerations for IP performance metrics rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: Two Audiences for Performance Reports
sections.content:
The RFC asks how measurement results will be used and identifies two audience categories. Network characterization describes conditions inside a network for troubleshooting, quality assurance, modeling, or service-level agreements. Application performance estimation describes network conditions to help predict their effect on users and applications.

The two points of view affect test parameters and reported statistics. The memo focuses on long-term reporting, including hours, days, weeks, or months, and covers loss, delay, delay variation, reordering, and capacity metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: Network operators may use measurements to diagnose the network, while application designers may use them to estimate user experience. The report should state enough about its purpose and method for readers to interpret it.

sections.title: Combining Short Measurements into Long Reports
sections.content:
A measurement interval and a reporting interval do not need to have the same length. The RFC recommends using shorter measurement intervals within a longer reporting period rather than running one measurement continuously without saving intermediate results. Short intervals limit the effect of power failures, timing outages, and maintenance on the collected record.

Results can be combined by storing every individual result, using temporal aggregation, or comparing each interval with an objective and reporting the fraction of time that meets it. The RFC notes that numerical acceptability thresholds are outside its scope. It recommends reporting loss and delay for periods when connectivity can be demonstrated and separately summarizing periods without demonstrated connectivity.
sections.plainLanguage: Collect measurements in shorter intervals and combine them for the longer report. This preserves intermediate results if the measurement system stops or loses synchronization.

sections.title: Loss and the Waiting Time
sections.content:
A loss metric uses a waiting-time threshold: a packet that has not arrived by that time is classified as lost. Network characterization benefits from a long wait because routing loops during convergence may cause unusually long delays. The RFC calculates a worst-case example of about 51 seconds and says approximately 50 seconds is manageable in practice.

Application-specific thresholds are often shorter, but they can be applied after measurement by reclassifying packets whose delay exceeded the application's limit. The RFC also recommends distinguishing packets that never arrive from errored packets that arrive, when the measurement system can do so.
sections.plainLanguage: A longer waiting time helps separate very late packets from packets that never arrive. A later analysis can apply a shorter limit for an application that cannot use those late packets.

sections.title: Delay for Packets That Do Not Arrive
sections.content:
The one-way delay metric leaves delay undefined for a packet that does not arrive. The RFC recommends retaining that distinction and reporting delay conditional on packet arrival. Applications handle arrived packets differently from missing packets, and treating missing packets as infinitely delayed would count the same problem in both loss and delay.

For delay, the RFC recommends reporting both the mean and median of the conditional distribution. It notes that minimum, maximum, and percentile values can add context. For delay variation, it recommends using the minimum delay as the reference and gives a high-percentile-minus-minimum value as a useful summary.
sections.plainLanguage: A missing packet has no measured arrival delay, so report it as lost rather than as infinitely late. This keeps the loss and delay results from counting the same packet twice.

sections.title: Raw and Restricted Capacity
sections.content:
Raw capacity metrics describe capacity without restrictions such as data uniqueness or congestion control. IP-layer capacity, utilization, and available capacity form a related set: knowing two constrains the third. Restricted capacity includes Bulk Transfer Capacity (BTC), which counts unique payload bits delivered over time by a congestion-aware connection.

Reports should describe the measurement method and its parameters, including packet or segment characteristics, duration, and any maximum the measurement can assess. The RFC recommends reporting variability with minimum, maximum, range, a maximum-to-minimum ratio, moving averages, or plots of individual results over time. It notes that a commonly used utilization interval is 5 minutes and can conceal variability.
sections.plainLanguage: Capacity can describe the network's raw ability to carry IP traffic or the useful data delivered by a congestion-aware transfer. Reports should name the method and show how results vary over time.

sections.title: Test Streams, Sample Size, and Security
sections.content:
Reports should describe the test stream and sample size. A stream resembling the application may help estimate application performance, while other stream patterns may suit network characterization. The RFC says sample size should be chosen with the expected variability, desired confidence, and impact of measurement traffic in mind.

Active measurements on live networks carry security considerations. Long-term tests keep ports open longer and may be easier to detect. Long packet waiting times also give an attacker more opportunity to prepare a replay attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Describe how test packets were sent and how many results were collected. Long measurements and long waits also create security considerations for the measurement system.
